newsitem.title: CHINA: First British ship in 10 years calls at China port.
newsitem.headline: First British ship in 10 years calls at China port.

text.p: The British destroyer HMS Exeter sailed into the north China port of Qingdao on Monday, the first British naval vessel to visit in a decade and marking an improvement in Sino-British ties, officials said.
"It is a goodwill visit," said Captain Paul Herington after the Exeter sailed into the naval base at Qingdao to be greeted by a small Chinese navy band playing under cloudy skies.
"It is to get to know a little better our friends in the People's Liberation Army, and the navy in particular, as part as part of the deepening of Sino-U.K. relations," he said.
The ship, with its complement of 280 sailors on board, would remain in Qingdao until October 11, officials said.

The sailors would be able to go on shore to explore the former German treaty port of Qingdao, renowned for its Tsingtao beer that has been brewed for decades to a German recipe, and some would go sightseeing in Beijing, officials said.
"This is the first visit by a Royal navy ship to China for 10 years," the embassy said in a statement. "It reflects a steady improvement in relations between Britain and China."
British naval vessels previously visited Shanghai in 1980 and 1986.

Relations between China and Britain plunged in the early 1990s after Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten introduced electoral reforms in the British colony that Beijing said violated the terms of the agreement on the handover of the territory to China.
Ties have improved substantially over the last year, with Hong Kong -- a treaty port like Qingdao -- due to revert to Beijing sovereignty at midnight on June 30, 1997.
The British sailors seemed surprise at the wave of modernisation in Qingdao.
"I didn't think it would be so built up," said 21-year-old sailor Tom Saunders. "I thought it would be a little town rather than big buildings. I thought it would be more rundown."
